harbor.practice: Harbor retrieves current expense limits at query time; a small fine-tune only fixed answer formatting.
harbor.failure: Putting private facts into model weights and assuming deleting the source document removes them.
harbor.fitNote: changing, permissioned policies are a knowledge problem
harbor.tryIt: Classify five Harbor gaps as knowledge or behaviour: a new expense limit, the mandated answer format, an acronym the model misreads, a policy only some staff may see, and a tone complaint. Decide prompt, RAG or fine-tune for each.

store.fitNote: prices, stock and listings change daily
store.practice: {company}'s listings, prices and stock change constantly, so {assistant} retrieves them at question time. A small fine-tune taught the reply style (short, friendly, order ID first) that prompting kept getting wrong.
store.failure: Fine-tuning on the catalogue so the model “knows” products. Prices go stale the next day, and deleted listings cannot be removed from the weights.
store.tryIt: List five facts {assistant} needs (price, stock, return window, size chart, delivery estimate) and five behaviours (tone, language, length, order ID first, escalation), and mark each as retrieval, tool or fine-tune.

bank.fitNote: the topic's own example: weekly-changing policies plus a format fine-tune
bank.practice: The topic's example is a bank: {company} retrieves its weekly-changing policies with citations and role filters, and used a small fine-tune only for the mandated “Decision / Basis / Exceptions” format.
bank.failure: Putting customer-specific facts into a fine-tune. They cannot then be deleted on request.
bank.tryIt: Write the knowledge-versus-behaviour table for {company}'s dispute assistant using policies.json and disputes.csv.

travel.fitNote: fares and disruptions change by the minute
travel.practice: Fares, seat availability and disruption notices are knowledge that changes by the minute, so they come from tools and retrieval. How {assistant} phrases a rebooking offer is behaviour, tuned separately.
travel.failure: Expecting a fine-tuned model to know today's disrupted flights.
travel.tryIt: Classify ten traveller questions (from messages.json and your own) as knowledge, served by retrieval or a tool, or behaviour, served by a prompt or fine-tune.

harbor.practice: Harbor keeps each reimbursement limit and its exception in the same chunk, with a parent link to the full section and the policy's effective date as metadata.
harbor.failure: Trying to fix poor PDF parsing by switching to a stronger answer model.
harbor.fitNote: each limit stays in the same chunk as its exception
harbor.tryIt: In the chunking figure, compare fixed-size 40-word chunks with paragraph-aware chunking and find a rule separated from its exception. Then chunk the texts in policies.json and check every limit stays with its exception.

store.fitNote: listings, size charts and policy pages chunk differently
store.practice: {company}'s documents are short listings, long size charts and policy pages. Listings are indexed whole with attributes as metadata; size charts are split by table section with the product category in every chunk's header.
store.failure: Chunking a size chart by fixed word count, which separates the size column from the measurements.
store.tryIt: Write the chunk header (category › product › section) for three products in products.csv, and decide whether each listing needs chunking at all.

bank.fitNote: policy chunks carry IDs, effective dates and audience
bank.practice: {company}'s policy chunks carry the policy ID, effective date, product and audience as metadata, and each chunk is prefixed with its section path, so “the limit is 1 lakh per day” is never ambiguous.
bank.failure: Indexing scanned policy PDFs with poor OCR and then blaming the answer model for wrong limits.
bank.tryIt: Chunk the texts in policies.json with a section-path header and effective date, and write the metadata record for one chunk.

travel.fitNote: a fee and its exception must stay together
travel.practice: {company} chunks fare rules so a fee and its exception (“no changes within 4 hours”) stay in one chunk, with the fare family and product in the header.
travel.failure: Fixed-size chunks that split “changes allowed for a fee” from “not within 4 hours of departure”.
travel.tryIt: Chunk the saver-fare rules in fare_rules.json by hand into 15-word windows, find where a fixed size separates a rule from its exception, then re-chunk by sentence with a header.

harbor.practice: Harbor's BM25 leg finds error codes like E-4012 and part numbers; the dense leg finds "can't get into my account" → "authentication recovery".
harbor.failure: Assuming a vector database chooses a good embedding model for you; it only stores and searches vectors.
harbor.fitNote: error codes for BM25, paraphrases for dense search
harbor.tryIt: Choose “HTTP 429” and then “cannot log in” in the BM25 figure and explain each result. Then run bm25s over policies.json with “PTO carry over”.

store.fitNote: SKUs, sizes and brand names are keyword territory
store.practice: Shoppers type exact things: “UK 8”, a SKU, a brand name. BM25 finds those instantly; dense retrieval handles “shoes for a wedding” and Hinglish paraphrases. {company} runs both.
store.failure: Relying on dense retrieval alone and missing exact SKU and size matches.
store.tryIt: Index the titles in products.csv with bm25s and search “UK 8 sneakers” and one SKU; then repeat with a small embedding model and compare the top three results.

bank.fitNote: references from SMS alerts versus paraphrased complaints
bank.practice: Customers quote transaction references and error codes from SMS alerts; BM25 finds those exactly, while dense retrieval matches “money cut but payment failed” to the failed-UPI policy.
bank.failure: Expecting an embedding model to match a 12-digit reference number.
bank.tryIt: Run BM25 and a multilingual embedding model over policies.json for the Hinglish “paise kat gaye payment fail” and for “UPI debit reversal”, and compare.

travel.fitNote: airport codes and fare-family names are exact tokens
travel.practice: Airport codes, booking references and fare-family names are exact tokens for BM25; dense retrieval matches “can I shift my trip” to the change rules.
travel.failure: Lowercasing and stemming airport codes into common words in the keyword index.
travel.tryIt: Search fare_rules.json for “saver change fee” with BM25 and with embeddings, and for the exact phrase “48 hours”.

harbor.practice: Harbor measures its HNSW index against exact search (ANN recall) and, separately, against human relevance labels (retrieval quality).
harbor.failure: Raising ANN recall to fix a representation that ranks the wrong passages close to the query.
harbor.fitNote: ANN recall measured separately from relevance
harbor.tryIt: Run the HNSW figure five times and compare its distance computations with the 300 of brute force. Then compute memory for 2 million 768-dimension vectors in float32 (about 6.1 GB) and int8 (about 1.5 GB).

store.fitNote: millions of listings need ANN and compression
store.practice: {company} has millions of listing vectors, so search uses HNSW over int8 vectors and re-scores the top 200 with full precision. efSearch was tuned on real shopper queries against exact search.
store.failure: Tuning efSearch on random vectors instead of real shopper queries.
store.tryIt: Embed the 300 titles in products.csv, run exact and FAISS HNSW search for 20 queries, and measure HNSW's Recall@10 against exact search at two efSearch values.

bank.practice: {company}'s policy corpus is small (thousands of chunks), so exact search is fast enough and avoids explaining approximate results in audits.
bank.failure: Adding an ANN index to a small corpus and then having to justify its approximate results to auditors.
bank.tryIt: Time exact cosine search in NumPy over embeddings of policies.json and the dispute texts, and confirm it takes milliseconds.

travel.practice: Fare rules are few; hotel descriptions are many. {company} uses ANN only for the hotel catalogue.
travel.failure: Using one ANN configuration for every collection regardless of its size.
travel.tryIt: Estimate memory for 1 million hotel-description vectors of 384 dimensions in float32 (about 1.5 GB), int8 and binary, using the figure's ratios.

harbor.practice: Harbor fetches 50 lexical + 50 dense candidates under the user's ACL filter, fuses with RRF, reranks the top 30 and assembles 5 non-duplicate passages.
harbor.failure: Adding raw BM25 and cosine scores together; their scales mean different things.
harbor.tryIt: In the RRF figure, set k to 5 and then to 100 and watch doc-C and doc-F. Then write Harbor's pipeline as code with the ACL filter inside both searches, not after them.

store.fitNote: stock, pincode and category filters inside the search
store.practice: {company} fuses BM25 and dense results with RRF, filters by stock, delivery pincode and category inside the search, and reranks the top 50 with a cross-encoder trained on clicks.
store.failure: Post-filtering by stock after retrieving 20 results, leaving shoppers with two.
store.tryIt: Fuse BM25 and dense rankings for “red cotton kurta under ₹1000” over products.csv with RRF (k = 60), applying the price filter before fusion and then after, and compare.

bank.fitNote: product and role filters keep rules from mixing
bank.practice: {company} applies the customer's product and role filters inside retrieval, so a credit-card question never retrieves another product's dispute rules, then reranks and assembles cited clauses.
bank.failure: Adding raw BM25 and cosine scores to rank policy clauses. The scales mean different things.
bank.tryIt: Implement RRF over BM25 and dense lists for three queries over policies.json, and check whether the fused order beats each list by your own relevance judgement.

travel.practice: {assistant} filters fare rules by the booking's product and fare family inside search, so a saver-fare question cannot retrieve flex rules.
travel.failure: Retrieving across all fare families and letting the model pick, which mixes up change fees.
travel.tryIt: Add product and fare-family metadata to the entries in fare_rules.json, and write the filter a saver-fare flight booking should apply.

harbor.practice: "Can my team claim this?" makes Harbor resolve "this" from history, look up the user's region and role, then retrieve both the base policy and the regional exception, or ask a clarifying question.
harbor.failure: Citing a whole 80-page document when the answer depends on one clause.
harbor.tryIt: Write the standalone rewrite for “Can my team claim this?” given a two-turn history. Then check citations in code: every cited ID must exist among the retrieved chunks.

store.fitNote: follow-up questions about the product in view
store.practice: “Does it come in blue?” is rewritten with the product from the chat before retrieval. Comparison questions are decomposed per product, and answers cite listing and review IDs; if nothing supports an answer, {assistant} says the listing does not say.
store.failure: Citing the whole listing page when the answer depends on one attribute line.
store.tryIt: Write rewrites for three follow-up questions about one product in products.csv, plus an abstention message for an attribute the listing lacks.

bank.fitNote: deadline questions need the transaction and the rule
bank.practice: {company}'s questions are often two-hop: “What is my dispute deadline?” needs the transaction's statement date, then the policy's 30-day rule. Each hop is cited, and a failed hop leads to abstention.
bank.failure: Answering a deadline from the policy alone, without the transaction's date, which gives a generic and possibly wrong date.
bank.tryIt: For a case in disputes.csv, write the two hops (transaction lookup, then policy lookup) and the cited answer; then remove the transaction and write the abstention.

travel.fitNote: questions that span a booking and a rule
travel.practice: “Can I get a refund if my flight is cancelled for fog?” needs the booking's fare family, then the weather-disruption rule. {assistant} decomposes it, retrieves both and cites them.
travel.failure: Answering from the general weather rule without checking the booking's fare family.
travel.tryIt: Decompose that question into hops over bookings.csv and fare_rules.json, then write the cited answer and the abstain path if the booking is not found.

harbor.practice: Harbor reports Recall@10 on 300 pooled, labelled real queries per release, with per-query diffs for anything that regressed.
harbor.failure: Reading retrieval metrics as answer quality; they do not measure whether the answer was supported.
harbor.fitNote: Recall@10 on 300 pooled, labelled real queries
harbor.tryIt: In the metrics figure, move the grade 3 result up to rank 1 and watch reciprocal rank and nDCG rise while Recall@k stays the same. Then label five queries over policies.json and compute Recall@10.

store.fitNote: plentiful shopper queries give cheap pooled labels
store.practice: {company} labels retrieval with pooled results from BM25, dense and hybrid for 300 real shopper queries, and tracks Recall@10 and nDCG@10 per language and query type (SKU, attribute, vague).
store.failure: Labelling only the old retriever's results, which penalises a new retriever for finding different good results.
store.tryIt: Pool the top 5 from BM25 and dense for 10 queries over products.csv, label relevance 0–3 yourself, and compute Recall@5 and nDCG@5 for each retriever with both gain conventions.

bank.fitNote: only the first cited clause usually gets read
bank.practice: {company} reports MRR for policy questions, because customers and agents read the first cited clause and rarely look further.
bank.failure: Reporting Recall@20 when only the first two passages ever reach the letter.
bank.tryIt: Label the relevant policy for ten dispute questions from disputes.csv and compute MRR for BM25 over policies.json.

travel.fitNote: one right rule per question, graded relevance for hotels
travel.practice: {company}'s fare-rule queries have one right rule each, so Recall@3 and MRR are the main numbers; hotel search uses graded nDCG.
travel.failure: Reporting graded nDCG without stating the gain convention, so two teams' numbers cannot be compared.
travel.tryIt: Compute nDCG@3 with linear and exponential gains for one hotel query using relevance grades you assign, and note the difference.

harbor.scenario: Use policies.json as the corpus (tenant labels from access_groups) and write queries from tickets.csv. Include exact identifiers (error codes, order IDs) and paraphrases, and check that outdated revisions are not counted as relevant.

store.scenario: Use the listings in products.csv as documents. Queries include SKUs, sizes (“UK 8”), brand names, vague requests and Hinglish questions; report metrics per query type.

bank.scenario: Use policies.json plus 20 short product documents you write. Turn dispute texts from disputes.csv into queries, including Hinglish ones, and report MRR alongside Recall@k.

travel.scenario: Use fare_rules.json plus 30 short hotel descriptions you write. Queries come from messages.json and change or refund questions; each fare-rule query has exactly one relevant rule.
